pages.text: The Wizard of Oz

image.note: Cover: Dorothy, Toto, and the yellow brick road

pages.text: Contents. The Cyclone / The Land of Oz / Three Friends / The Emerald City / The Wicked Witch / There's No Place Like Home.

Dorothy lived on a flat grey farm in Kansas with her aunt, her uncle, and her little dog Toto. It was a plain and quiet life, until the day a great whirling storm picked up the whole house, dog, girl, and all, and carried it up, up, and far away.

image.note: The little grey farmhouse under a dark sky

pages.text: A cyclone is a wind that spins, and this one was the strongest anyone had seen. Uncle and Aunt ran for the storm cellar, but Toto slipped from Dorothy's arms, and by the time she caught him, the house was already rising, spinning, into the heart of the storm.

image.note: The house lifting into the spinning storm

pages.text: Round and round the house whirled, high in the sky, yet inside, Dorothy found it strangely gentle, like being rocked in a cradle. She grew sleepy, curled up on her bed with Toto, and, high above the earth in a flying house, fell fast asleep.

image.note: Dorothy asleep in the flying house

pages.text: A great bump woke her. The house had come down softly, in a land more beautiful than any she had seen: green and bright, full of flowers and birdsong. This was not Kansas. Dorothy opened the door, looked out, and gasped. "Toto," she said, "I don't think we are at home any more."

image.note: Dorothy opening the door onto colourful Oz

pages.text: A crowd of little people came to greet her, the Munchkins, and with them a kind old woman, a good witch. "You have saved us," they cried, for the falling house had landed on a wicked witch who had ruled them cruelly, and set the Munchkins free. Dorothy had not meant to, but she was a hero.

image.note: The Munchkins greeting Dorothy

pages.text: "But how do I get home?" asked Dorothy. "You must go to the Emerald City," said the good witch, "and ask the great Wizard of Oz. He is the only one wise enough to help you. Follow the road of yellow brick." She gave Dorothy a magic kiss for protection, and a pair of silver shoes from the fallen witch.

image.note: The good witch pointing to the yellow brick road

pages.text: So Dorothy set off, Toto trotting beside her, along the road of yellow brick. It wound through a lovely country, and she wondered what the great Wizard would be like, and whether he really could send a girl and her little dog all the way home to Kansas.

image.note: Dorothy and Toto on the yellow brick road

pages.text: Along the way she made three friends, each looking for something. First a Scarecrow, stuffed with straw, stuck on a pole in a field. Dorothy helped him down. "I have no brains, only straw," he sighed. "Come with me to the Wizard," said Dorothy, "and perhaps he will give you some." And the Scarecrow gladly came.

image.note: Dorothy helping the Scarecrow down

pages.text: Next they found a man made all of tin, rusted stiff in the woods, who could only squeak until Dorothy oiled his joints. "I have no heart," said the Tin Man sadly, "and I should so like one, to love with." So he joined them too, his axe on his shoulder, marching for the Emerald City.

image.note: Dorothy oiling the rusted Tin Man

pages.text: Last of all, out of the forest sprang a great Lion with a mighty roar, who then burst into tears. "I am a dreadful coward," he wept. "A lion is meant to be brave, and I am afraid of everything." "Then come and ask the Wizard for courage," said Dorothy. And now they were four friends and a dog together.

image.note: The Cowardly Lion joining the group

pages.text: At last, green and glittering on the horizon, rose the Emerald City, where everything shone the colour of emeralds. The friends were brought, one by one, before the great Wizard of Oz, and each found him terrifying and strange: a booming voice, a floating head, a ball of fire.

image.note: The glittering Emerald City

pages.text: "I will grant your wishes," boomed the Wizard, "home, brains, a heart, and courage. But first you must do something for me. Far in the west lives a Wicked Witch who troubles this land. Go, and put an end to her power, and then come back, and I will help you all."

image.note: The friends before the booming Wizard

pages.text: The friends were afraid, for the Wicked Witch of the West was cruel and strong. But they had no choice, and they had each other, and so they set off westward: a girl, a dog, a scarecrow, a tin man, and a lion, to face the most feared witch in all of Oz.

image.note: The four friends setting off west

pages.text: The Witch saw them coming with her one sharp eye, and sent wolves, and crows, and swarms of bees to stop them, but the Scarecrow and the Tin Man and the Lion beat them all back. At last, in a fury, she used a magic cap to call a swarm of winged monkeys, who seized the friends and carried them to her castle.

image.note: Winged monkeys seizing the friends

pages.text: The Witch made Dorothy her servant, and schemed to steal the silver shoes, for she knew they held a powerful magic. One day she tripped Dorothy and snatched one shoe. Dorothy, angry at the unfairness of it, seized a bucket of water and threw it over the wicked old Witch.

image.note: Dorothy throwing water at the Witch

pages.text: And that, it turned out, was the one thing the Witch could not bear. With a great cry she began to melt, away and away, until nothing was left of her but a puddle and an empty cloak. The friends were free, and the whole land she had ruled rejoiced. The task was done.

image.note: The Witch melting away

pages.text: Back they went to the Emerald City, proud and triumphant. But when they demanded their reward, Toto knocked over a screen in the corner, and behind it stood, not a floating head or a ball of fire, but an ordinary little old man, pulling levers. The great and terrible Wizard was no wizard at all.

image.note: Toto revealing the man behind the screen

pages.text: "I am only a humbug," the old man admitted. But he was a clever and kindly one. He showed the Scarecrow he had been thinking cleverly all along, the Tin Man that he loved deeply already, the Lion that he had been brave all through. What they wanted, he said, they had carried inside them from the start.

image.note: The little Wizard reassuring the three friends

pages.text: "But I still must get home," said Dorothy. The Wizard tried to help, but it was the good witch Glinda who knew the secret. "Your silver shoes can carry you anywhere," she told Dorothy. "They could have taken you home from the very first day. You had only to ask them."

image.note: Glinda telling Dorothy about the shoes

pages.text: So Dorothy hugged each of her friends goodbye, the Scarecrow, the Tin Man, the Lion, holding Toto tight. Then she knocked the heels of the silver shoes together three times, and said the words: "There's no place like home. There's no place like home."

image.note: Dorothy clicking the silver heels together

pages.text: In a whirl of wind she was lifted up, and set down, gently, on the grey Kansas farm, in her aunt's arms, Toto barking at her side. She had seen a land of wonders, and made the truest friends, but oh, it was good to be home. For however marvellous the road, there really is no place like it.

image.note: Dorothy home in Kansas, hugging her aunt

pages.text: The friends of Oz. Dorothy, who only wanted to go home. Toto, her faithful dog. The Scarecrow, who wanted brains. The Tin Man, who wanted a heart. The Lion, who wanted courage. And each of them, in the end, found that what they most wanted was theirs all along.

image.note: Montage of the Oz friends
